title: Angulimala, read whole
hookLine: the story from year one, now read in full

lines: TOLD IN PIECES, NOW READ WHOLE.
cards: Pasenadi of Kosala rides out of his capital with five hundred horsemen. His people have been gathering outside the palace, crying out about a killer in the forest, and the king is going to hunt Angulimāla down.
On the way, he stops to pay respects to the Buddha. In year one, around day seventy, I told this story in pieces: the road, the chase, I have stopped, the woman in labor, the stones.
Now the eighty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, read whole, and quieter scenes like this one come into view.

teach.b: The Buddha asks him: what's wrong, great king? Is a neighboring kingdom attacking you? No, says Pasenadi.
It's a bandit, Angulimāla. I'm going to put him down. Then the Buddha asks an unexpected question.
Suppose you saw Angulimāla with his head shaved, in robes, gone forth, gentle, eating one meal a day, keeping the precepts.

teach.h: WHAT IF HE WERE A MONK?
teach.b: What would you do? The king says: I'd bow to him, offer him robes and food and shelter, and protect him. But how could someone like that ever become someone like this?
The Buddha stretches out his arm and points.
There is Angulimāla. The king is terrified, his hair standing on end. Don't be afraid, the Buddha says.
You have nothing to fear from him. The king walks over, asks his family name, and offers him robes. Angulimāla says he already has his three.
The king turns back to the Buddha and says it plainly: the one we couldn't tame with punishment or weapons, you've tamed without either. And he rides home.
The sutta goes on: the woman in labor, the stones on the alms round, and then Angulimāla alone, freed, speaking verses.
One is also in the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's words: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds."
In another verse he says his name had been Harmless, and now, at last, he lives up to it. Read whole, the story isn't only about one man stopping. A king stops too.

how: Angulimāla's verse of truth for a safe birth, the Aṅgulimāla Paritta, is still chanted by monks in Theravada countries for expectant mothers, and his story is told as proof that anyone can change.

o: a monk who carried stones to build the temple walls
a killer who stopped, and lived up to the name Harmless
a forest bandit the king's army finally captured

games.q: the sutta, read whole: tap the pairs.
p: rode out with five hundred horsemen
what if you saw him as a monk?

s: King Pasenadi captured and punished Angulimāla
he found him a monk, offered him robes, and rode home.
the king says the Buddha tamed him without punishment or weapons
the one we couldn't tame with rod or sword, you tamed without either.
one of Angulimāla's verses is also in the Dhammapada
the moon freed from clouds, verse 172 in Müller's numbering.

games.q: you're King Pasenadi, riding out to kill a bandit. the Buddha asks: what if you found him shaved, robed and gentle? what does the king answer?
o: I'd bow to him and offer him robes and food
games.why: the king says he'd honor him. then the Buddha points: there he is. a king on a hunt ends up offering robes.

practice: If you have the Dhammapada or the sutta nearby, open it and read a few lines aloud, slowly; if not, say Müller's moon verse once, at the pace of a walk: he who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds.
Then sit quietly with the picture of the moon coming out from behind a cloud.

wordCard.voice: Angulimāla. The killer who stopped, read whole: the Buddha on the road, the king with his army, and a man who finally lived up to his name, Harmless.

orig.note: Pali ṭhito ahaṃ: 'I have stopped', the Buddha's answer on the road.

carryVoice: Your line: I have stopped. Tamed without punishment or weapons. Day four hundred seventy-one, done.
